questions.question: How is an improper integral, over an infinite interval or of an unbounded integrand, defined?
options: By substituting $\infty$ into an antiderivative
As a Riemann integral over $[a,\infty)$ directly
As an area that is always finite
As a limit of ordinary definite integrals

questions.question: Which improper integral converges?
options: $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^0\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x$
$\displaystyle\int_1^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d}x}x$
$\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt x}$

questions.question: When does an improper integral converge?
options: When every required limit exists as a finite real number
When the defining limit exists, even if it equals $+\infty$
When the integrand tends to $0$ at the infinite endpoint
When the integrand is bounded on the interval of integration

questions.question: Besides an infinite endpoint, which behaviour at an endpoint of a bounded interval makes an integral improper?
options: The integrand becomes unbounded near that endpoint.
The integrand has a single jump there and is otherwise continuous.
The derivative of the integrand becomes unbounded near that endpoint.
The endpoint is left out, as in $(0,1]$, while the integrand stays bounded and continuous.

questions.question: Which statement about $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,\mathrm{d}x$ is correct?
options: It converges to $0$, since $\int_{-R}^{R}x\,\mathrm{d}x=0$ for every $R>0$
It diverges, since $\int_{0}^{\infty}x\,\mathrm{d}x$ already diverges
It converges, since $x$ is continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}$
It is a proper integral, since $x$ is bounded on every bounded interval

questions.question: A student writes $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}=\Bigl[-\frac{1}{x}\Bigr]_{-1}^{1}=-2$. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The value $-2$ is right, because $-\frac{1}{x}$ is an antiderivative of $\frac{1}{x^2}$
The value should be $2$; only the sign is wrong
The integral converges, since the problem point $0$ is interior, not an endpoint
The integral diverges, since $\int_0^1\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}$ diverges

questions.question: Let $p\in\mathbb{R}$ and consider the improper integral $\displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}x^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}x$ of the function $x^{-p}$, defined for $x>0$. For which values of $p$ does this integral converge?
options: For $0<p<1$ only
For $p>1$ only
For every $p\neq1$
For no real $p$
